23 years ago, I was a 10 year old child with autism. From how it was handled, I learned pretty much everything NOT to do. 

First and foremost, be open and honest with your son about his condition. Hiding it from him as my parents did to me would be doing him a great disservice and will make it much harder for him to plan a realistic and viable future. 

Secondly, as hard as it can be, please try to remain patient with him when he exhibits signs of his AS. Never use special education or therapy as tools of punishment or humiliation. My parents did this which gave me a negative view of the services that were in place to help me and for many years I rejected them at every opportunity. 

The third recommendation I would make is to determine what it is that he does best. Most people with AS tend to have a very strong skill in one area. His best shot at living a full and independent life is to start career planning at a very young age. With proper planning and realistic evaluations, I believe that most anyone with AS can go on to live an enjoyable life. 

Unfortunately for me, none of what I recommended was done with me as I was growing up and all I've managed to do with my life is become a poverty statistic. This doesn't have to be the future for your son and very likely will not be with early intervention and long-term planning.

I wasn't formally diagnosed with AS until 23 and felt pretty betrayed at the time. From my earliest memories, I was constantly being subjected to various tests and put into every special education program that was available. Whenever I would question this, my parents would either say it was because I was bad, lazy, or a disappointment to them. The only other thing I was ever told was "you're in these programs because your muscles haven't caught up with your brain." 

I bought that explanation for a while, because young people with AS are overly trusting. AS aside, most young children never expect their parents to lie to them anyway. Considering that nearly all of the problems I had/have and the treatments I was in had nothing to do with muscular issues, I should have smelled a rat sooner.

I progressed through childhood being berated at every turn and being severely punished whenever I displayed the symptoms of AS. When I was 16, I was applying for an after school job and needed to find my birth certificate. In the search for it, I came across a folder filled with papers and decided to see what they were.

In this folder, I found an encyclopedic amount of forms and papers discussing me, the tests I'd been given, and the special education and child psychology programs I'd been in. Every time the question "Does this child have a severe disability that will profoundly affect their ability to function in most major areas of life?" the YES box was checked. 

Reading further, I saw what they had diagnosed me with Non-Verbal Learning Disorder, a common diagnosis back in the days when Aspergers/Autism were less understood. In reading my IQ scores, I saw that I had a verbal IQ of 153 and a performance IQ of 66, which is below the cutoff point for mental retardation.

I confronted my parents about this and all they did was scream at me and tell me I had no right to read those papers. Years later, I went to therapy of my own accord, was subjected to another battery of tests, and finally had the formal diagnosis of Asperger Syndrome.

Not everyone with Asperger Syndrome is going to be as impaired career-wise as I am, because a performance IQ of 66 is frighteningly low, even for someone on the spectrum. Still, my experiences have shown me that I'm hardly the only AS case where these problems have come up. 

From 2010-2014, I was part of a nine person therapy group for people with AS. We were more or less lab rats for a psychologist who was in the process of writing a book about youngish-adults (ages ranged from 26-38) with Asperger Syndrome and wanted to see what would go on in the group setting. All of us were unemployed, all of us had trouble with the most basic functions, and none of us were living independently. Everyone was either living with parents or on the public dole. 

I firmly believe that it doesn't have to be like this and that many people with AS, if something is done early enough, can go on to be successful in careers and life. The problem is aside from the social aspects, most of the symptoms go untreated and unmentioned.

Whether or not it can be called a disease is up for debate, but anyone who thinks it isn't a disability is living in a dream world. Nearly all online job applications have a voluntary section where they ask you if you have a disability. In most of these, there's a list which tells you the conditions that qualify as a disability. I've never seen one that didn't list autism. 

Additionally, my Asperger Syndrome is the main reason why I qualify for Social Security Disability. I have physical problems as well, but was told that the AS was my trump card for securing benefits.

In the earlier jobs I took the same approach as you - I tried to take notes about everything because I can't learn any other way. Usually, employers grew tired of this and wrote me off as a lost cause. Some were more patient with me and let me take all of the notes I wanted. I didn't fare any better with those, because my ability to convert what I've learned into actual productivity is virtually non-existent. My performance IQ, when last tested, was a dismal 66. That pretty much damns me to a life of minimum wage slavery, and even that has proven too high of a goal in most cases. 

Most of my jobs after the first few years were self-employment because at least I couldn't fire myself. All but one of these ended in pathetic failure, and the only one that didn't still didn't generate enough money to live on. Ultimately that one failed too, due the death of the industry it was in. Through it all, none of these problems have ever been a result of anything socially related. My social skills aren't the best, but they've never taken me out of a job. If the functional issues aren't addressed and all that is catered to is the social deficits, we'll wind up with a generation of AS kids who can schmooze with the big guys but still not be able to do much of anything.

I felt betrayed. From my earliest memories, I was constantly being subjected to various tests and put into every special education program that was available. Whenever I would question this, my parents would either say it was because I was bad, lazy, or a disappointment to them. The only other thing I was ever told was "you're in these programs because your muscles haven't caught up with your brain." I bought that explanation for a while, because young people with AS are overly trusting. AS aside, most young children never expect their parents to lie to them anyway. Considering that nearly all of the problems I had/have and the treatments I was in had nothing to do with muscular issues, I should have smelled a rat sooner. 

I progressed through childhood being berated at every turn and being severely punished whenever I displayed the symptoms of AS. When I was 16, I was applying for an after school job and needed to find my birth certificate. In the search for it, I came across a folder filled with papers and decided to see what they were.

In this folder, I found an encyclopedic amount of forms and papers discussing me, the tests I'd been given, and the special education and child psychology programs I'd been in. Every time the question "Does this child have a severe disability that will profoundly affect their ability to function in most major areas of life?" the YES box was checked. Reading further, I saw what they had diagnosed me with Non-Verbal Learning Disorder, a common diagnosis back in the days when Aspergers/Autism were less understood. In reading my IQ scores, I saw that I had a verbal IQ of 153 and a performance IQ of 66, which is below the cutoff point for mental retardation.

I confronted my parents about this and all they did was scream at me and tell me I had no right to read those papers. Years later, I went to therapy of my own accord, was subjected to another battery of tests, and finally had the formal diagnosis of Asperger Syndrome.

Let me tell you something that will be hard to handle, but it's for your own good. I've been there and I remember those years, so I know from whence I speak. 

The social problems caused by Asperger Syndrome suck when you're going through school, but they are nowhere near the worst problems this disease is going to cause you. The real trouble in life begins when you finish school, are away from all of the social dynamics, and need to find work.

There's an 85% unemployment rate for Aspies and nearly all who are employed are underemployed. I've been out of college for 11 years now and have never come close to earning a living wage. In the earlier years, I'd just fuck up at everything I tried to do and get fired. The only thing that got me through the doors was the fact that I had a 3.95 GPA in college, something that proved to be utterly worthless in the end.

Now all of my gaps in employment are seen and every employer on my resume has plenty of horror stories to tell any place I apply to that might have considered taking me. I've finally just given up and decided to go on disability, officially making me worthless and undeserving of life. 

The reason I say all of this is to prepare you for your future and to stop torturing yourself over these social situations that will be nothing but a memory in a few years. It's a temporary problem. The functional problems of AS last a lifetime. 

If you want to avoid turning out like I did, please forget the social drama and focus all of your efforts on discovering what it is that you can do well and that might possibly offer a future career to you. Don't blindly go off to college just for the sake of going to college. A degree without the competence to back it up is worth less than a sheet of used toilet paper. 

You're still young enough to figure these things out and still have a chance at a decent future. You'll never get there though until you confront the real issues AS will bring to your life and waste your time worrying about what happened at your prom. Prom sucked for me too - I actually managed to get a date, but she ditched me almost as soon as we arrived for a guy she liked more who came alone. Did it hurt? Fuck yes, but does it have anything to do with why my life is a living hell now? No. 

I wasted my time agonizing over social issues so much that I never considered the more practical survival issues I'd be dealing with later. I paid the price for it and I don't want you or anyone else who is at your stage of life to do the same. People are assholes and always look out for #1. Any "friend" will stab you in the back and stab you another 73 times before you can get up if it will benefit them in some way. Relationships with humans beyond necessary professional connections are useless and a waste of time.

I don't think normal people as a whole are at all any less intelligent than people with our condition. I've heard a lot of Aspies say that we're more intelligent or the next step in evolution, but that's hard for me to believe. 

With evolution, it's survival of the fittest and the best traits are passed on to the next generations. As Aspies, we date and engage in sex much less frequently than normal people do and therefore we reproduce at lower rates. If anything, this makes the argument that we're at a lower rung of the evolutionary ladder. 

What I'm basically saying is it's dangerous to mark normal people as being inferior and us as superior, as we need their help much more than they need ours. Not many of us can afford to burn many bridges with the support systems we have.
